questions.question: What is a ResultSet in JDBC and how do you iterate it?
questions.title: JDBC ResultSet — Iterating Query Results
questions.direct_answer: A **ResultSet** is a **cursor** over the rows returned by a query. It starts positioned **before the first row**; you call **`next()`** to advance (it returns `false` when rows run out) and `getXxx("col")` to read columns. It's forward-only by default and must be closed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know ResultSet is a cursor and the next()/getXxx iteration loop.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reading a column before calling next(), or assuming it's a loaded list.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note the cursor starts before row 1 and ResultSet is forward-only by default.

sections.title: What a ResultSet Is and How to Iterate
sections.content:
A **`ResultSet`** is a **cursor** (not a loaded list) over the rows a SELECT returns. The cursor begins **before the first row**, so you must call **`next()`** first — it moves to the next row and returns `true`, or `false` when there are no more rows. Inside the loop you read columns with `getInt`, `getString`, etc., by **column name** or **1-based index**.

By default a `ResultSet` is **forward-only** and tied to its `Statement`/`Connection`, so you read it once and **close** it (try-with-resources).

sections.title: ResultSet at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~a cursor|over query rows|not a loaded list|tied to its Statement
emerald|Iterate|~next() loop|starts before row 1|next() returns true/false|getXxx to read
amber|Read columns|~by name or index|getString("name")|getInt(1)|1-based index
rose|Default|~forward-only|read once|close when done|try-with-resources

sections.title: Iterating a ResultSet
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reading before `next()`**: the cursor starts before the first row — always call `next()` first.
- **Treating it as a list**: it's a forward cursor, read once.
- **Using it after closing the Statement/Connection**: the ResultSet becomes invalid.
- **0-based column index**: indices are 1-based (`getInt(1)`).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **ResultSet** is a cursor over query rows.
- **Starts before the first row** — call `next()` before reading.
- **`next()`** advances and returns `false` when done.
- **Read** with `getXxx` by column name or 1-based index.
- **Forward-only by default**; close it (try-with-resources).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A ResultSet is a cursor over the rows that a query returns. It's important to understand it's a cursor, not a fully loaded list in memory; it points at one row at a time. The cursor starts positioned before the first row, which is the key detail people forget. So to read data, you first call next, which moves the cursor to the next row and returns true if there's a row there, or false when you've run off the end. That's why the standard pattern is a while loop on rs dot next. Inside the loop, you read each column with the typed getters, like getInt and getString, and you can read either by column name, which is more readable, or by a one-based column index. By default a ResultSet is forward-only, meaning you iterate through it once from start to finish, and it's tied to the Statement and Connection that produced it, so once those are closed the ResultSet is invalid. That's why you close it when you're done, ideally with try-with-resources. The mistakes to avoid are trying to read a column before calling next, since the cursor starts before the first row, treating the ResultSet like a reusable list, and using zero-based column indices when they're actually one-based.

questions.question: How do you check for NULL values when reading from a ResultSet?
questions.title: Checking NULL Values in JDBC ResultSet
questions.direct_answer: Numeric getters like `getInt`/`getLong` return **0** for a SQL NULL, which is ambiguous. To detect a real NULL, call **`rs.wasNull()`** right after the getter, or use **`getObject`** (which returns Java `null`). This distinguishes 'value is 0' from 'value is missing'.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know primitive getters return 0 for NULL and how to detect it.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating a returned 0/false as a real value when the column was NULL.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use wasNull() immediately after the read, or getObject for nullable columns.

sections.title: Checking for NULL in a ResultSet
sections.content:
JDBC's primitive getters can't represent NULL: **`getInt`/`getLong`/`getDouble` return 0** and `getBoolean` returns `false` when the column is SQL **NULL** — indistinguishable from a real 0 or false. To tell them apart:

- Call **`rs.wasNull()`** **immediately after** the getter — it reports whether the last read column was NULL.
- Or use **`getObject(col)`** / wrapper-returning getters, which return Java **`null`** for a NULL.

For object getters like `getString`, a NULL already comes back as `null`, so this mainly matters for primitives.

sections.title: NULL in ResultSet at a Glance
sections.content:
rose|Primitive getters|~0 for NULL|getInt -> 0|getBoolean -> false|ambiguous
blue|wasNull()|~the check|call right after getter|true if last read was NULL|positional
emerald|getObject|~returns null|Integer / null|clean for nullable cols|preferred
amber|String getters|~already null|getString -> null|no wasNull needed|

sections.title: Ambiguous: 0 might be a real value or NULL
Clear: use wasNull() or getObject
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Trusting a returned 0/false**: it may be a NULL, not a real value.
- **Calling `wasNull()` too late**: it refers to the *last* column read — call it right after.
- **Mapping nullable columns to primitives**: use wrappers/`getObject`.
- **Forgetting `getString` returns null**: object getters already handle NULL.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Primitive getters return 0/false** for SQL NULL — ambiguous.
- **`rs.wasNull()`** (right after the getter) detects a NULL read.
- **`getObject`** returns Java `null` for NULL — cleaner for nullable columns.
- **`getString`** already returns `null` for NULL.
- **Don't map nullable columns** to primitives.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Checking for NULL in a ResultSet matters because JDBC's primitive getters can't actually represent a NULL. If a numeric column is SQL NULL, getInt and getLong return zero, getDouble returns zero point zero, and getBoolean returns false. The problem is that's indistinguishable from a genuine zero or false in the data, so you can't tell whether the value was really zero or was actually missing. There are two clean ways to handle this. The first is to call rs dot wasNull immediately after the getter; it reports whether the last column you read was NULL. The key detail is that wasNull refers to the most recent read, so you have to call it right after the getter, before reading anything else. The second, and usually cleaner, approach is to use getObject, which returns a Java object that's null when the column is NULL, so you can just check for null. For object-returning getters like getString, this isn't an issue, because getString already returns null for a NULL column; the ambiguity only affects the primitive getters. So my practice is to never map a nullable column to a primitive; I either check wasNull right after the read or use getObject, so I can clearly distinguish a real zero from a missing value.

questions.question: What is ResultSet TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY vs TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE?
questions.title: ResultSet Types — Forward-Only vs Scrollable
questions.direct_answer: **TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY** is the default — you can only move the cursor forward with `next()`, which is fast and memory-light. **TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE** lets you move the cursor freely (`previous`, `absolute`, `first`) and isn't affected by others' changes, but uses more resources.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the two ResultSet types and their trade-offs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Requesting a scrollable ResultSet by default when forward-only suffices.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note 'insensitive' means it ignores concurrent changes; prefer forward-only for performance.

sections.title: TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY vs TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE
sections.content:
JDBC lets you choose how the cursor moves. **`TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY`** (the default) only goes **forward** via `next()` — minimal memory, maximum speed, and the right choice for normal sequential reads. **`TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE`** is **scrollable**: you can call `next`, `previous`, `first`, `last`, `absolute(n)` to move anywhere. *Insensitive* means it takes a snapshot and **ignores concurrent changes** made by others while you scroll — but it holds more in memory.

Use forward-only unless you genuinely need to scroll backward or jump around.

sections.title: ResultSet Types at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|FORWARD_ONLY|~default|next() only|fast + low memory|sequential reads
blue|SCROLL_INSENSITIVE|~scrollable|previous/absolute/first|snapshot, ignores changes|more memory
amber|Insensitive meaning|~stable snapshot|others' edits not seen|consistent scroll|
rose|Choose|~by need|scroll? -> scroll type|else -> forward-only|don't over-request

sections.title: Forward-Only vs Scroll-Insensitive
sections.content:
| Aspect | TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY | TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE |
|---|---|---|
| Movement | forward only (`next`) | any direction |
| Methods | `next()` | `previous`, `absolute`, `first`, `last` |
| Memory/cost | low | higher |
| Sees others' changes | n/a | no (snapshot) |
| Default | yes | no |

sections.title: Forward-only (default) — sequential
Scroll-insensitive — move anywhere
When to Use Which
sections.content:
Use **`TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY`** for the vast majority of queries — you read rows once, top to bottom. It's the fastest and lightest.

Use **`TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE`** only when you must navigate backward, jump to a specific row, or count rows via `last()`/`getRow()` — and you're fine with a snapshot that ignores concurrent edits.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY** (default): `next()` only, fast, low memory.
- **TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE**: move any direction (`previous`, `absolute`).
- **Insensitive** = snapshot, ignores others' concurrent changes.
- **Scrollable costs more memory.**
- **Prefer forward-only** unless you truly need to scroll.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: These are two cursor types for a ResultSet that control how you can move through the rows. TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY is the default, and as the name says, you can only move forward, using next. It's fast and uses minimal memory because the driver doesn't have to keep rows around for backward navigation, and it's the right choice for the normal case where you just read rows once from top to bottom. TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE makes the ResultSet scrollable, so you can call next, previous, first, last, and absolute to jump to any row, move backward, or count rows. The insensitive part of the name means it works off a snapshot and ignores concurrent changes that other transactions make while you're scrolling, so what you see stays consistent during your scroll. The trade-off is that a scrollable ResultSet holds more in memory and costs more. To request it, you pass the type and a concurrency mode when you create the statement. So the guidance is straightforward: use forward-only for the vast majority of queries because it's the fastest and lightest, and only reach for scroll-insensitive when you genuinely need to navigate backward, jump to specific rows, or get a row count via last and getRow. The mistake is over-requesting a scrollable cursor by default when forward-only would do.

questions.question: How do you map ResultSet rows to Java objects in JDBC?
questions.title: Mapping ResultSet to Java Objects in JDBC
questions.direct_answer: To map a `ResultSet` to Java objects, iterate it and for each row read the columns and construct your object — typically inside a reusable **RowMapper** (`ResultSet → T`). This keeps mapping logic in one place; Spring's `JdbcTemplate` formalizes the same pattern.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can convert rows into domain objects cleanly.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Inlining mapping everywhere, duplicating column reads and bugs.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Extract a RowMapper; mention Spring JdbcTemplate uses exactly this abstraction.

sections.title: Mapping ResultSet Rows to Objects
sections.content:
Database rows are flat columns; your app wants **objects**. The pattern: loop with `next()`, read each column, and build a domain object per row, collecting them into a `List`. To avoid duplicating that read-and-construct logic, extract it into a **RowMapper** — a small function `ResultSet -> T` that maps one row.

This is exactly the abstraction **Spring's `JdbcTemplate`** uses (`RowMapper<T>`), letting you write the mapping once and reuse it across queries.

sections.title: Row Mapping at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Pattern|~loop + build|next() per row|read columns|construct object
emerald|RowMapper|~ResultSet -> T|one place for mapping|reusable|testable
amber|Collect|~into a List|add per row|return list|or Optional for one
rose|Spring|~same idea|JdbcTemplate RowMapper|query(sql, mapper)|less boilerplate

sections.title: Mapping Recipe
sections.content:
| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | run query → `ResultSet` |
| 2 | `while (rs.next())` |
| 3 | read columns, build object |
| 4 | add to `List<T>`, return |

sections.title: A reusable RowMapper
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Inlining mapping everywhere**: duplicates column reads; extract a RowMapper.
- **Column name typos**: a wrong name throws at runtime — keep mapping centralized.
- **Ignoring NULLs**: use `getObject`/`wasNull` for nullable columns.
- **Building objects before `next()`**: read only after advancing the cursor.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Loop** with `next()`, read columns, build an object per row.
- **Extract a RowMapper** (`ResultSet -> T`) for reuse.
- **Collect** into a `List<T>` (or `Optional<T>` for one).
- **Spring `JdbcTemplate`** uses the same `RowMapper` pattern.
- **Handle NULLs** with `getObject`/`wasNull`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Mapping a ResultSet to Java objects is about turning flat database columns into your domain objects. The basic pattern is to loop with next, and for each row read the columns and construct an object, adding each one to a list that you return. That works, but if you inline that read-and-construct logic in every query, you end up duplicating column reads and it's easy to introduce bugs. So the cleaner approach is to extract a RowMapper, which is just a small function that takes a ResultSet positioned on a row and returns one object of your type, a ResultSet to T mapping. You write the mapping once and reuse it across queries, which also makes it easy to test. For example, I'd define a User record and a userMapper lambda that reads id, name, and email from the current row and builds a User, then in my query loop I just call the mapper for each row. This is exactly the abstraction Spring's JdbcTemplate provides with its RowMapper interface; you pass a RowMapper to jdbcTemplate dot query and it handles the iteration for you, so you write far less boilerplate. A couple of things to keep in mind while mapping: centralize it to avoid column-name typos scattered everywhere, and for nullable columns use getObject or check wasNull so you handle NULLs correctly instead of getting a default value.

questions.question: What happens if you do not close a ResultSet in JDBC?
questions.title: Consequences of Not Closing ResultSet in JDBC
questions.direct_answer: An unclosed `ResultSet` leaks resources — it holds a **database cursor** and memory on both client and server. Leaks accumulate and can exhaust cursors/connections, eventually causing errors or hangs. The fix is **try-with-resources**, which closes the `ResultSet` automatically, even on exceptions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know unclosed ResultSets leak cursors and the try-with-resources fix.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Relying on Statement/Connection close or GC to clean up the ResultSet.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note closing the Statement closes its ResultSet, but explicit try-with-resources is clearest.

sections.title: What Happens If You Don't Close a ResultSet
sections.content:
A `ResultSet` holds real resources: a **database cursor** on the server and buffers on the client. If you don't close it, those resources aren't released promptly — a **leak**. Under load, leaked cursors accumulate until you hit the database's **open-cursor limit** or exhaust connections, causing errors or hangs.

Closing a `Statement` or `Connection` does close its `ResultSet`, but relying on that (or on garbage collection, which is non-deterministic) is fragile. The robust fix is **try-with-resources**: declare the `ResultSet` in the `try(...)` and it closes automatically, even if an exception is thrown.

sections.title: Unclosed ResultSet at a Glance
sections.content:
rose|Leak|~holds resources|DB cursor + buffers|not released|accumulates
blue|Symptom|~under load|open-cursor limit hit|errors/hangs|hard to spot in tests
amber|GC not enough|~non-deterministic|don't rely on it|close explicitly|
emerald|Fix|~try-with-resources|auto-close|even on exception|reverse order

sections.title: Leak-prone: ResultSet not closed on error
Safe: try-with-resources closes the ResultSet
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Unclosed ResultSet** leaks a DB cursor + client buffers.
- **Leaks accumulate** → hit open-cursor limits → errors/hangs.
- **GC is non-deterministic** — don't rely on it.
- **Closing the Statement** closes its ResultSet, but be explicit.
- **try-with-resources** closes it safely, even on exceptions.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: If you don't close a ResultSet, you leak resources, because a ResultSet holds a real database cursor on the server side plus buffers on the client side. When you fail to close it, those resources aren't released promptly. One unclosed ResultSet won't hurt, but under load they accumulate, and eventually you can hit the database's limit on the number of open cursors, or exhaust connections, which shows up as errors or the application hanging. It's a sneaky bug because it's invisible with a couple of rows in a test and only surfaces under real traffic. Now, technically, closing the Statement or the Connection will also close any ResultSet it produced, so people sometimes rely on that. But relying on it is fragile, and relying on garbage collection is worse, because GC is non-deterministic and the cursor could stay open for a long time. The robust fix is try-with-resources: you declare the ResultSet, and ideally the PreparedStatement too, in the parentheses of the try, and Java guarantees they're closed automatically when the block exits, in reverse order, even if an exception is thrown in the middle of processing. That makes the cleanup deterministic and removes the leak entirely, which is why I always use try-with-resources for ResultSets.

Using JPA and thinking this doesn't apply — Hibernate opens JDBC ResultSets internally; it closes them but misconfigured lazy loading can leave them open.

speakable_v2.cap: Always close ResultSets explicitly. try-with-resources is the safest one-line way to guarantee it.

questions.question: What is ResultSetMetaData and how do you use it?
questions.title: ResultSetMetaData Usage
questions.direct_answer: **ResultSetMetaData** describes the **structure** of a ResultSet — column count, names, types, and labels — obtained via `rs.getMetaData()`. It's used to process queries **generically** when you don't know the columns ahead of time, like building a CSV export or a dynamic grid.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know ResultSetMetaData exposes column structure for generic processing.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Hard-coding column names when the query shape is dynamic.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use getColumnCount + getColumnLabel/getColumnType to iterate columns generically.

sections.title: What ResultSetMetaData Is For
sections.content:
**`ResultSetMetaData`** describes a ResultSet's **shape** rather than its data: how many columns, their **names/labels**, their **types**, precision, nullability. You get it with `rs.getMetaData()`.

It shines when you **don't know the columns at compile time** — generic tools like CSV/Excel exporters, admin query runners, dynamic UI grids. Instead of hard-coding column names, you loop from 1 to `getColumnCount()` and read each column's label and value generically.

sections.title: ResultSetMetaData at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~describes structure|column count|names/labels|types + nullability
emerald|Get it|~from the ResultSet|rs.getMetaData()|after executeQuery|
amber|Use|~generic processing|unknown columns|CSV/export|dynamic grids
rose|Key methods|~iterate columns|getColumnCount()|getColumnLabel(i)|getColumnType(i)

sections.title: Generic Processing Recipe
sections.content:
| Step | Method |
|---|---|
| 1 | `ResultSetMetaData md = rs.getMetaData()` |
| 2 | `int cols = md.getColumnCount()` |
| 3 | loop `i = 1..cols`: `md.getColumnLabel(i)` |
| 4 | `rs.getObject(i)` for the value |

sections.title: Printing any ResultSet generically
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Hard-coding columns for dynamic queries**: use metadata to discover them.
- **0-based column loop**: columns are 1-based (`1..getColumnCount()`).
- **Confusing name vs label**: `getColumnLabel` returns the alias (`AS`), `getColumnName` the underlying column.
- **Assuming types**: read `getColumnType` if you need type-aware handling.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **ResultSetMetaData** describes columns: count, names, types.
- **Obtained** via `rs.getMetaData()`.
- **Use for generic processing** when columns are unknown.
- **`getColumnCount` + `getColumnLabel`** drive a 1-based loop.
- **`getColumnLabel`** = alias; `getColumnName` = real column.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: ResultSetMetaData describes the structure of a ResultSet rather than its actual data. It tells you how many columns there are, their names and labels, their data types, precision, and whether they're nullable. You get it by calling rs dot getMetaData after running your query. Where it really earns its place is when you don't know the columns at compile time. For example, if you're building a generic CSV or Excel exporter, an admin tool that runs arbitrary queries, or a dynamic data grid, you can't hard-code column names because they change per query. Instead, you ask the metadata for getColumnCount, then loop from one to that count, and for each column read its label with getColumnLabel and its value with getObject. That lets you process any query generically without knowing its shape in advance. A few details worth knowing: the column indices are one-based, so the loop runs from one to getColumnCount inclusive. And there's a distinction between getColumnLabel, which returns the alias you gave a column with AS, and getColumnName, which returns the underlying column name, so I pick whichever I actually want to display. If I need to handle values differently based on type, I can also read getColumnType. So in short, ResultSetMetaData is the tool for column-agnostic, generic result processing.

questions.question: What is a scrollable ResultSet and when would you use one?
questions.title: Scrollable ResultSet
questions.direct_answer: A **scrollable ResultSet** lets the cursor move in any direction — `next`, `previous`, `first`, `last`, `absolute(n)` — rather than forward-only. You request it via `createStatement(TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE, ...)`. Use it when you must navigate backward, jump to specific rows, or count rows with `last()/getRow()`; otherwise prefer forward-only.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know how to create and when to use a scrollable ResultSet.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using scrollable cursors by default, wasting memory.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note scrollable types cost more memory; pagination is usually better than scrolling.

sections.title: What a Scrollable ResultSet Is
sections.content:
A **scrollable ResultSet** can move the cursor **freely**, not just forward. With it you can call `previous()`, `first()`, `last()`, and `absolute(n)` to jump to any row. You enable it by passing a scroll type when creating the statement: `con.createStatement(ResultSet.TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE, ResultSet.CONCUR_READ_ONLY)`.

It's useful for backward navigation, random access to specific rows, or quickly getting a row count via `last()` then `getRow()`. The cost is **higher memory** (the driver buffers rows), so for normal sequential reads, **forward-only** is better — and for large data, **pagination** usually beats scrolling.

sections.title: Scrollable ResultSet at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~free cursor movement|previous/first/last|absolute(n)|not forward-only
emerald|Enable|~at statement creation|TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE|CONCUR_READ_ONLY|then executeQuery
amber|Use when|~need navigation|backward reads|jump to a row|count via last()/getRow()
rose|Cost|~more memory|driver buffers rows|prefer forward-only|paginate for big data

sections.title: Creating and using a scrollable ResultSet
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Defaulting to scrollable**: wastes memory; use forward-only unless you need scrolling.
- **Scrolling huge results**: prefer SQL pagination (LIMIT/OFFSET or keyset).
- **Forgetting to set the type**: the default is forward-only — `previous()` then throws.
- **Assuming it sees live changes**: `INSENSITIVE` is a snapshot.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Scrollable** = move any direction (`previous`, `absolute`, `last`).
- **Enable** with `TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE` at statement creation.
- **Use for** backward/random navigation or row counts.
- **Costs more memory** — prefer forward-only normally.
- **For big data**, paginate instead of scrolling.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A scrollable ResultSet is one where the cursor can move in any direction, not just forward. With a normal forward-only ResultSet you can only call next, but with a scrollable one you can also call previous to go backward, first and last to jump to the ends, and absolute to jump to a specific row number. You enable it by passing a scroll type when you create the statement, specifically TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE along with a concurrency mode like CONCUR_READ_ONLY, and then you run your query. It's handy in a few situations: when you need to navigate backward, when you need random access to particular rows, or when you want a quick row count by calling last and then getRow. The downside is that a scrollable ResultSet costs more memory, because the driver has to buffer rows to support moving around, so for the common case of reading rows once from top to bottom, forward-only is more efficient and is what I default to. I also point out that for large datasets, scrolling isn't really the right tool; SQL-level pagination with LIMIT and OFFSET, or better yet keyset pagination, is usually the better approach than pulling everything into a scrollable cursor. And one nuance: the insensitive part means it's a snapshot, so it won't reflect changes other transactions make while you scroll.

seo.metaDescription: Scrollable ResultSet types: forward-only vs scroll-insensitive vs scroll-sensitive. Why SQL pagination is preferred. Java backend fresher interview answer.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app connecting to a MySQL database with JDBC to query an orders table
speakable_v2.hook: A scrollable ResultSet lets you jump to the last row to count, then leap to row 3 — handy, but you buy that freedom with memory.

beats.text: You're choosing between needing random access to rows in a result set (scrollable) or just iterating through rows once top to bottom (forward-only). For pagination specifically, you're choosing between client-side row buffering and server-side SQL pagination.

items: TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY — default; rows are streamed; only next() works; memory-efficient for any size dataset
TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE — all rows buffered in memory; previous(), absolute(n), first(), last() all work; snapshot of data at query time
SQL LIMIT/OFFSET — let the database return only the rows you need; no buffering; the modern pagination approach

beats.text: Use forward-only for every normal query. If you need page-based access to rows, write SQL with LIMIT and OFFSET — the database returns only what you need. Scrollable ResultSets are a legacy feature rarely needed in modern applications.

items: You're using TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE to count rows via rs.last(); rs.getRow() — use a COUNT(*) SQL query instead.
You're buffering a large result set for backward navigation — that data belongs in a paginated query, not in application memory.

speakable_v2.cap: Forward-only is almost always right. If you need pagination, do it in SQL. Scrollable ResultSets are for edge cases in legacy code.
